## Why the same prompt gives different answers
- LLM output is sampled. Unless `temperature` is 0, or very low with `topP` pinned, answers will differ run to run. Even at temperature 0 you shouldn't expect bit-identical output, because serving-side numerics can still vary.
- If the model ID is a cross-Region inference profile (the `us.` prefix), requests can be served from different Regions. That is another possible source of variation.
- Different answers on their own say nothing about model health.

## Why 0.82 → 0.79 may not be a regression
- If the job generates answers with sampling on, each run scores a different set of outputs, even on a fixed dataset.
- If any metric uses an LLM judge, the judge adds its own variance. For Nova LLM-as-judge runs, AWS reports `*_stderr` and bootstrap bounds (`lower_rate` and `upper_rate`). A difference inside those bounds is noise, not a regression.
- With a small dataset, one or two prompts changing outcome can move the score by about 0.03.

## How to tell noise from regression
1. Re-run the identical job 3–5 times with the same model, dataset and config. The spread of those scores is your noise band. If 0.79 falls inside the band of the 0.82 runs, there's no regression.
2. Compare the two weekly jobs' configs: model ID and inference profile, `inferenceParams`, dataset S3 object version, judge model, metrics and task type. Any difference there explains the delta without a model change.
3. Check whether the dataset object changed. A dataset that is "fixed" but overwritten in place is a common cause.
4. Check the finish-reason distribution in the invocation logs. If `max_tokens` truncations rose by more than 10 percentage points against baseline, that is a real quality signal and it points to a prompt length or `maxTokens` change. Output token counts rising while invocations stay flat is an early warning of the same thing.
5. Look at per-prompt results, not just the aggregate. If a handful of prompts flipped and the rest are unchanged, that is noise. If one category dropped across the board, that is a regression.

## How to make it reproducible
- Pin the inference settings in the evaluation job itself: `temperature: 0`, fixed `topP` and `maxTokens`. For SageMaker Nova recipes, set `temperature: 0` in the `inference` block.
- Pin the exact model ID, and the judge model if you use one. Record both in each run's metadata.
- Version the dataset immutably (S3 versioning or a per-run prefix). Store each run's dataset, config and output under a prefix keyed by run ID and model version (check LLM-EVAL-008).
- Use repeated runs and a tolerance gate instead of a single comparison. Run the job N times, compare mean ± stderr, and fail promotion only when the candidate falls below baseline by more than the measured noise band (LLM-EVAL-007).
- Publish each score to CloudWatch as a custom metric with model and version dimensions, so you can see a trend instead of two points (LLM-EVAL-005).
- Compare candidate and incumbent on the same dataset in the same run window (LLM-EVAL-006).

Whether a real regression exists in production, as opposed to in the evaluation score, is not determined. I haven't looked at live traffic, and live-failure triage wasn't part of this check.
